stem: On a learning curve, what is on the horizontal axis?
choices: Output per period
Number of workers
Cumulative production
Price
explain: Experience = cumulative production (slide p. 32). Output per period is what economies of scale depend on.

choices: Users value a product more as more people use it
Average cost declines as output per period increases
Output rises as more workers are hired
Cost per unit declines as cumulative production increases
explain: Learning = declining costs per unit; experience = cumulative production.

stem: True or false: An 80% learning curve means unit cost falls by 80% each time cumulative output doubles.
choices: True
False
explain: False. It falls TO 80% of its old level, a 20% drop, with each doubling.

stem: Which strategic implication of learning curves appears on the S18 slides?
choices: Firms should produce less to keep costs low
Learning curves make predatory pricing legal
Learning curves eliminate the need for economies of scale
Firms may price aggressively to descend the learning curve faster
explain: Selling more now builds cumulative output faster, which lowers future costs (slide p. 34).

stem: Three learning curves start at the same cost. Which is the weakest barrier to entry?
choices: One where the incumbent is far down a long curve
One that drops almost all the way in the first few units and then goes flat
One where knowledge cannot leak to rivals
One that keeps falling over a long range of cumulative output
explain: If nearly all the learning happens in the first few units, an entrant gets there quickly too, so the incumbent's lead is short.

stem: The first unit costs $1,000 and the firm is on an 80% learning curve. What does the 8th unit cost?
The first unit costs $500 on a 90% learning curve. What does the 4th unit cost?
The Model T cost curve on the slides is \(y = 87{,}244x^{-0.317}\). By what factor does unit cost change each time cumulative production doubles? Round to 2 decimals.
explain: \(2^{-0.317} = 0.80\): about an 80% learning curve, a 20% drop per doubling.

stem: The 100th unit costs $200 on an 85% learning curve. What does the 400th unit cost?
A solar panel maker's cost per panel fell 20% each time its total panels ever produced doubled. A rival hires away several of its process engineers. What happens to its learning-curve barrier?
choices: Nothing changes; learning is about cumulative output only
It turns into economies of scale
It weakens, because knowledge spills over to the rival
It strengthens, because the rival now has higher costs
explain: Learning effects are a barrier only if there is no knowledge spillover or leakage (slide p. 34, Quiz 8 Q2).

stem: A shipyard's cost per ship fell from $90 million on its 1st ship to $60 million on its 20th, even though it builds only two ships a year. Which concept explains this?
choices: Learning curve
Economies of scale
Network effects
Economies of scope
explain: Output per year did not grow; cumulative experience did. That is the learning curve, not scale.

stem: A chip maker cuts prices on a new memory chip below its current unit cost to sell huge volumes in its first year. Which reason fits the S18 slides?
choices: Descend the learning curve faster to lower future costs
Predatory pricing to drive out an existing rival
Limit pricing, since the price is above cost
Penetration pricing to build network effects
explain: Slide p. 34: firms may price aggressively to move down the learning curve faster. No rival or network is mentioned.
